one_liner: LiteSpeed's C QUIC + HTTP/3 client/server library; LSQUIC-to-LSQUIC bulk downloads beat quiche-to-quiche 1.2-1.5x at 10 Gbit/s.
what_it_does: A C library that implements QUIC (v1, v2, draft-29, and legacy gQUIC Q043/Q046/Q050, which are off by default) along with HTTP/3 and QPACK, for both servers and clients. The same code runs in LiteSpeed Web Server, LiteSpeed ADC and OpenLiteSpeed. The API is event-driven and leaves I/O to you: you create a client-mode or server-mode engine with lsquic_engine_new() and register stream callbacks and an ea_packets_out send function. Your code owns the UDP sockets, passes received datagrams to lsquic_engine_packet_in(), and calls lsquic_engine_process_conns() when lsquic_engine_earliest_adv_tick() says a connection is due. It is a separate API, not a replacement for quiche.
how_it_is_fast: The internals doc states the rule outright: 'performance trumps everything else'. On the send path, the engine interleaves packets from every connection into one batch and hands it to ea_packets_out, which makes sendmmsg-style sending possible. The batch grows toward 1024 while sends succeed and shrinks after a partial send. On the receive path, ACK merging combines consecutive ACK frames and processes them once per tick (the docs say this cuts ACK-processing calls 10-20x), and the delayed-ACK extension uses a PID controller to set packet tolerance. As a result the LSQUIC client sends far fewer ACKs: in the paper, quiche's client sent more than 16x as many. Other hot-path choices: fixed-size 'malo' pool allocators on 4 KB-aligned pages (the docs measured them 2.7x faster than malloc for 64-byte objects), stream data written straight into outgoing packets that are repackaged rather than rebuilt on loss, min-heap connection queues, and small 'mini' connections that handle the handshake.
when_to_use: You need an HTTP/3 or raw QUIC server or client in C, with a production record behind it (it ships in LiteSpeed's web servers), and bulk transfer throughput matters.
You control both ends. The measured win is for LSQUIC-LSQUIC pairs: about 3.0 Gbit/s with default settings and about 3.9 Gbit/s after tuning, on a 10G link.

Your app runs a single-threaded event loop per engine (libevent/libev style) and wants to own its sockets, or plug in its own packet-buffer allocation. The tumi8 LSQUIC-DPDK fork, for example, rewrote LSQUIC's packet allocation to write into DPDK mbufs.
You want broad protocol coverage in one library: QUIC v2, compatible version negotiation, unreliable datagrams, ACK frequency, HTTP priorities, and WebTransport (a build option).
Receive-side CPU or ACK traffic is a concern. Its ACK policy sends far fewer ACKs than quiche's did in the paper.
when_not_to_use: Serving clients you don't control, especially quiche-based ones. An LSQUIC server with a quiche client reached only 1186 Mbit/s (1616 after tuning), under half of the reverse pairing. The authors blame how the two libraries' flow control interacts.

You want the kernel's UDP segmentation or receive offloads (GSO/GRO) to do the heavy lifting. The same group's NOMS 2026 follow-up reports that LSQUIC uses neither, and there MsQuic reached 8250 Mbit/s vs LSQUIC's 3605. Code search finds no UDP_SEGMENT or UDP_GRO in the repo.

You plan to run BBR on low-RTT links. The paper saw LSQUIC with BBR reach only 30-70% of its Cubic goodput, with extra retransmissions. The internals doc says BBRv1 'does not work well for very small RTTs', which is why the default adaptive mode picks Cubic below 1.5 ms RTT.
Heavy packet loss (4% or more). A user reported LSQUIC falling behind Linux TCP there (issue #142). It was closed as stale with no fix.
You want one engine shared across threads, a memory-safe implementation, or easy packaging. BoringSSL has to be built from source (it needs Go), and thread safety is not a documented guarantee.

integration.form: static lib (default) or shared lib (-DLSQUIC_SHARED_LIB=1), built with CMake
integration.dependencies: A TLS library: BoringSSL, built by hand (the README suggests tag 0.20250807.0). Since 4.3.2, CMake also detects an OpenSSL that exposes SSL_set_quic_tls_cbs, but the README does not document it. Also zlib and the ls-qpack and ls-hpack git submodules. libevent is needed only for the demo programs. Links with -lstdc++.
integration.min_toolchain: CMake 3.0+ for lsquic (current BoringSSL needs CMake 3.22 and Go). Builds with GCC, Clang or MSVC; no minimum C standard or compiler version is documented.
integration.platforms: README 'tested on' list: Linux (i386, x86_64, ARM), FreeBSD i386, macOS x86_64, iOS ARM, Android ARM, Windows x86_64. CI runs on Linux, macOS, Windows and FreeBSD.
integration.thread_safety: The docs don't say. Each engine is driven from a single thread. Global variables were removed in 2.20.0 so that separate engines can run on separate threads (issues #167 and #267), but the maintainers say their own use 'does not require strict thread-safety', and one user reported crashes from sharing an SSL_CTX across threads.

gotchas: If CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE is not set, CMake builds Debug (-O0 -g3, plus AddressSanitizer when compiling with clang), and the README's build commands don't set it. The paper's baseline LSQUIC binary was built this way. Pass -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release. Debug log calls stay compiled in even in Release unless you add -DLSQUIC_LOWEST_LOG_LEVEL=LSQ_LOG_INFO, which the CMakeLists leaves commented out.

Throughput depends on the UDP receive buffer size. With the 208 KiB Linux default the LSQUIC client dropped 11.4k packets. A larger SO_RCVBUF gave 8.7% more goodput and cut the client's ACKs from 180k to 46k.

Memory trade-offs: the malo pools never return their 4 KB pages until the allocator is destroyed, and the cached ACK used for merging takes 4 KB+, more than half the size of each full connection object.

The sendmmsg/recvmmsg paths in the sample programs (-g/-j), which people often copy, failed with EFAULT at the commit the paper used (issue #434, filed by the paper's authors). They were fixed only in 4.7.1 in May 2026 (PR #646). A separate sendmmsg buffer overrun for batches over 1024 was fixed in PR #607.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick LSQUIC when you want a mature C library with HTTP/3 built in, running over the normal kernel UDP stack, and you control both endpoints. Choose ngtcp2 or TQUIC if their catalogued wins over quiche on bulk transfer (ngtcp2, about 1.6x download) or request rate (TQUIC, about 2.4x) match your workload better. Choose the LSQUIC-DPDK fork if you can dedicate NICs to kernel bypass and need close to line rate (about 10.8 Gbit/s).
verified_claims_summary: A peer-reviewed TUM study (IFIP Networking 2023) ran 8 GB HTTP/3 downloads over a direct 10 Gbit/s link between AMD EPYC 7543 hosts (Debian Bullseye, kernel 5.10) with Cubic/Reno. LSQUIC-LSQUIC pairs averaged 3004 Mbit/s vs 2506 for quiche-quiche (about 1.2x), even though that LSQUIC was an unoptimized Debug (-O0) GCC build and quiche was built with cargo --release. With a 32x larger UDP receive buffer, LSQUIC built Release -O3 -march=native and quiche built with target-cpu=native, the numbers were 3882 vs 2590 (about 1.5x). GCC and Rust versions are not recorded, and TCP/TLS reached 8010 Mbit/s on the same link. A 2026 follow-up (LSQUIC v4.2.0 vs quiche 0.23.2, Xeon Gold 6421N) measured a smaller lead, 3605 vs 3241 Mbit/s.
status_note: Actively maintained and MIT-licensed: 4.10.0 came out 2026-09-13, the last commit was 2026-09-20, and it has about 1.9k stars. Treat the source and headers as the reference, because the internals guide still describes v2.29.6 and the repo's contributor guidance warns the API reference can lag the headers.
